title: Select, use and care for engineering measuring equipment

lessons.title: Measuring tools and when to use them
lessons.html:
Why accurate measurement matters

In farm equipment repair, small measurements make a big difference. A bearing that is 0.05 mm too loose on a shaft can fail. Brake discs, shafts, bushes and valve clearances all have limits set by the manufacturer. Choosing the right measuring tool and using it correctly helps you decide whether a part can be reused or must be replaced.

Common measuring equipment

ToolTypical accuracyUse
Steel ruleAbout 0.5 mmQuick lengths, marking out
Measuring tapeAbout 1 mmLong lengths, wheel track, frames
Vernier caliper0.02 mm or 0.05 mmOutside, inside and depth measurements
Digital caliper0.01 mm displaySame as vernier, easier to read
Outside micrometer0.01 mmPrecise diameters of shafts, pins
Feeler gaugesBlade thicknesses markedGaps such as valve clearances
Dial indicator0.01 mmRun-out, end float, alignment
Try squareChecks 90°Squareness of fabrications
Torque wrenchSet value in NmTightening bolts to specification
Pressure gaugeScale on dialTyre and hydraulic pressures

Choosing the right tool

  • Check the tolerance needed in the manual. If the limit is given to 0.01 mm, use a micrometer or dial indicator, not a rule.
  • Choose a tool with the right range. A 0 to 25 mm micrometer cannot measure a 40 mm shaft.
  • Use the right type: inside, outside or depth.
  • Consider access. A caliper reaches places a micrometer cannot.

Units

Most farm equipment uses metric units (mm, Nm, bar or kPa). Some older or imported machines use inches, pound-feet or PSI. Check the manual and use conversion tables when needed.

lessons.title: Using calipers, micrometers and gauges
lessons.html:
Taking accurate readings

General rules

  • Clean the part and the tool. Dirt and burrs give wrong readings.
  • Check the tool reads zero when closed, or zero it.
  • Measure at room temperature if possible. Hot parts expand.
  • Take more than one reading at different points and positions, for example across a shaft at 90°, to check for wear or ovality.
  • Read the scale straight on, not at an angle, to avoid parallax error.
  • Record readings straight away.

Vernier caliper

  1. Close the jaws and check the zeros line up.
  2. Open the jaws, place them squarely on the part and close gently. Do not force.
  3. Read the main scale in whole millimetres just before the vernier zero.
  4. Find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main scale line; that gives the fraction.
  5. Add them. Example: main scale 23 mm, vernier line 14 on a 0.02 mm vernier = 0.28 mm; reading 23.28 mm.

Micrometer

  1. Check zero with the anvils closed (or with a standard for larger micrometers).
  2. Turn the thimble until the spindle nearly touches the part, then use the ratchet so the measuring force is always the same.
  3. Read the sleeve: whole millimetres and half millimetres.
  4. Read the thimble: hundredths of a millimetre.
  5. Add them. Example: sleeve 12.5 mm, thimble 0.36 mm = 12.86 mm.

Feeler gauges

Slide the blade into the gap. The correct blade should slide with a light drag. If it is loose, try a thicker blade; if it will not go in, try a thinner one.

Dial indicator

Mount it on a magnetic base, set the plunger against the part with a little preload, set the dial to zero, then turn or move the part and watch the needle. The total movement shows run-out or end float.

Comparing with specifications

Compare your reading with the manual's limits. If it is outside the service limit, the part must be replaced or repaired. Report results to your supervisor.

lessons.title: Caring for measuring equipment
lessons.html:
Protecting accuracy

Measuring tools are precision instruments. Rough handling makes them inaccurate, and an inaccurate tool is worse than no tool because you trust a wrong reading.

Handling

  • Never drop measuring tools. If one is dropped, have it checked before use.
  • Do not use calipers as a scriber, spanner or hammer.
  • Do not over-tighten a micrometer; use the ratchet.
  • Never measure moving parts, such as a turning shaft on a lathe.
  • Keep tools away from grinding dust, welding spatter and magnets (except dial indicator bases).
  • Keep them separate from heavy hand tools in the toolbox.

Cleaning and storage

  • Wipe tools clean after use with a soft cloth.
  • Apply a light film of instrument oil to steel surfaces to prevent rust.
  • Store in their cases in a dry place.
  • Leave micrometer anvils slightly apart when stored so temperature changes do not put stress on them.
  • Remove or check batteries in digital tools.

Torque wrenches

  • Set to the required value and pull smoothly until it clicks; stop at the click.
  • Do not use it to loosen bolts.
  • After use, wind a click-type wrench back to its lowest setting, as the maker recommends.

Calibration

Calibration means checking a tool against a known standard and adjusting it if needed. Workplaces keep calibration records with dates and results. Check the calibration sticker before use. If a tool is out of date or gives doubtful readings, tag it and report it.

Recording measurements

Write readings clearly on the job card or inspection sheet with units, for example 'Shaft diameter 34.97 mm, limit 34.95 mm, OK'. Good records show the condition of the machine over time.

Key points

  • Select a tool with the accuracy and range the job needs.
  • Clean the part, zero the tool and read the scale straight on.
  • Take several readings at different positions.
  • Use the micrometer ratchet; never measure moving parts.
  • Clean, oil lightly and store tools in their cases.
  • Use only calibrated tools and record readings with units.
